core: Working definition of nutrition science: the study of how food and nutrients affect the body and health (attributed to the field's standard framing; OpenStax defines nutrition as the intake of food to meet the needs of the body)
Nutrients as the substances in food and drink the body uses, with the six classes named: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water
Food's two big jobs: supplying energy and providing building materials for the body
Nutrition science as evidence-based: studies, evidence, and the cautious pace of findings
The general relationship between diet and long-term health, stated factually
Who studies nutrition: dietitians, researchers, and food scientists
The honest framing: a young science (20th century) with old advice
supporting: Macronutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, water) vs micronutrients (vitamins, minerals)
USDA recognition that poor nutrition is linked to diabetes, obesity, and heart disease
WHO statement that unhealthy diets are a major risk factor for disease and disability
Dietitian role in care teams: assessing needs and developing nutrition plans
outOfScope: Chemistry and digestion detail of carbohydrates, proteins, fats (own topics)
Absorption, metabolism, and cellular depth (own topics; biology subject owns cellular depth)
Supplements and their regulation (own topic: nutrition:foundations:supplements)
The critical-thinking frame for evaluating fad diets and claims (own topic: nutrition:foundations:evaluating-nutrition-claims)

claims.claim: Nutrition science studies how food and nutrients affect the body and health. OpenStax Nutrition defines nutrition as the intake of food to meet the needs of the body, and nutrients as substances found in foods and beverages that are essential for survival.

The body needs six classes of nutrients: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, and water. Carbohydrates, fats, and proteins are energy-yielding macronutrients needed in large amounts, water is classified as a macronutrient, and vitamins and minerals are micronutrients needed in smaller amounts.
Food performs two main jobs for the body: it provides energy the body needs to function, digest food, grow, and move, and it supplies materials the body uses as building blocks.

Nutrition knowledge is built on evidence: evidence-based practice uses scientific evidence rather than anecdotal evidence, and only some nutrition information available online is vetted for accuracy and validity.

Diet is linked to long-term health: the USDA recognizes poor nutrition as a substantial factor in illness in the United States, linked to diabetes, obesity, and heart disease; the WHO states that unhealthy diets are a major risk factor for disease and disability and that healthy diets help protect against noncommunicable diseases including diabetes, heart disease, stroke, and cancer.

Modern nutrition science is a young science: most of its major advances, including the identification of essential vitamins and minerals, the first recommended dietary allowances, and modern food guides, came during the 20th century.
Dietitians and nutritionists are experts in the use of food and nutrition to promote health and manage disease; they assess clients' nutritional and health needs and develop nutrition plans.
Agricultural and food scientists research ways to improve the efficiency and safety of agricultural establishments and food products.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Nutrition guidance has shifted over the decades (for example, the first U.S. dietary goals in 1977 recommended reducing red meat, and the wording was later changed to emphasize limiting saturated fat), which can look like the science changing its mind.
positions: Early guidelines and single studies sometimes overreach, and later evidence refines them.
Evidence-based practice weighs the accumulated body of research rather than any single study or headline.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents nutrition science as cumulative and cautious: findings build slowly, a single study is a data point rather than a verdict, and guidance is revised as evidence grows. No specific food is demonized and no personal dietary recommendation is made.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources differ on whether water counts as one of the nutrient classes.
positions: Many textbook lists name six classes: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, and water (OpenStax classifies water as a macronutrient).
Some older lists count five classes and treat water separately.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the six-class list, which matches the OpenStax backbone (water as a macronutrient) and the USDA Nutrition.gov coverage of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals, with water covered separately on the same federal site.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft described this lesson as covering a 'foundational concept in Nutrition' without defining the science; no draft claim survived research, and all wording was replaced with sourced content.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generic draft with a sourced lesson: working definition of nutrition science, the six nutrient classes, food's two jobs (fuel and building blocks), the evidence-based method and cautious pace of findings, the diet-long-term-health relationship, and the people who study nutrition.
Kept energy measurement (calories per gram) and carbohydrate/protein/fat detail out of scope so sibling topics own them.
rightsIssues: OpenStax Nutrition (Nutrition for Nurses) content treated as REFERENCE_ONLY per subject source-map guidance; facts synthesized, no source wording reproduced.
USDA Nutrition.gov, WHO fact sheets, and BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook are government/public sources; facts used, no text reproduced.
OpenStax sections were read via Wayback captures (canonical OpenStax URLs registered); BLS pages were read via Wayback captures because bls.gov blocked direct fetch.
